sections.title: Hiring a campervan in Christchurch
sections.context: You will hear a man phoning a campervan company in Christchurch to book a hire.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Southern Trails Campervans, Priya speaking.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Oh, hello. I'd like to hire a campervan for a trip around the South Island, please. I'm flying into Christchurch from Calgary next month.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Lovely, you'll have a great time. Let me bring up the booking form. Could I take your surname first?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: It's Mackenzie.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Is that M-A-C, then K?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Almost. It's M-A-C-K-E-N-Z-I-E.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Thank you. And a contact number? A New Zealand mobile if you have one, otherwise whatever's easiest.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: I'll buy a local SIM card when I land, but my sister lives in Dunedin and she'll be coming with us for the first part. Her number's 021 884 5576.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: 021 884 5576. Great. So when would you like to pick the van up?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: My flight lands on Saturday 4 October, so I was hoping to collect it that afternoon.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Ah, I'm afraid our depot closes at noon on Saturdays, and it's closed all day Sunday. So the earliest option would be Monday morning.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Hmm. That means two nights in a hotel. Well, I suppose it gives me time to recover from the flight. Okay, Monday it is.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: So that's Monday 6 October, I'll put that in. And for how long did you want the van?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: I was thinking eight days, but I need to be back in Christchurch for a flight on the Wednesday, so I'd better say 9 days.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Nine days, returning on the fourteenth. That works. How many people will be travelling?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Three. My sister, my daughter and me.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Then I wouldn't take the two-berth. It's cheaper, but it's really only suitable for couples. I'd suggest the four-berth, which has a proper table and a small kitchen.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Yes, the four-berth sounds better. What does that cost?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: In summer it's 160 dollars a day, but you're travelling in October, which is the shoulder season, so the rate drops to 145 dollars a day.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: That's good news. Is the 145 a day the final price, or are there extra charges?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: That covers the van, unlimited kilometres and bedding. Extras are optional. Some people take camping chairs or a portable heater, and families often want a child seat.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: We've got our own chairs in the boot of my sister's car, but my daughter's only six, so I'll need a child seat, please.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: No problem, I'll add a child seat. It's free of charge, but I do need to know the age, which you've just told me.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Great. Is there a deposit?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: We take a bond on your credit card, which is released when you bring the van back in good condition. It's 500 dollars.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Sorry, did you say 5000?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: No, five hundred. Just 500.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Phew, that's a lot more reasonable. And where exactly is your depot? I'll be taking a taxi from the hotel.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: We're at 41 Sandown Road, in Sockburn. That's number four-one.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Sorry, is that 14?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: No, it's 41. Four and then one. You'll see a big blue sign on the fence.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Got it. And the postcode, so I can put it into the taxi app?

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Perfect. Is there anything I should bring on Monday?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Your driver's licence and your passport. Since your licence is in English, you don't need an international permit. And please remember that in New Zealand we drive on the left.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: I've done it before, but I'm sure I'll make a few mistakes at roundabouts. Any advice for the roads on the way to the lakes?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Take your time. Many of the roads are narrow and winding, and distances look short on the map but take longer than you think. I'd allow at least two hours for every hundred kilometres.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: That's very useful. And can I change the booking if my plans shift?

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: Yes, as long as you let us know a week before you collect the van. After that, there's a small fee.

transcript.speaker: Callum
transcript.text: Okay. Thank you very much for your help, Priya.

transcript.speaker: Priya
transcript.text: You're welcome. I'll send the confirmation email within the hour. Safe travels, Callum.

sections.title: Canal Frost Weekend
sections.context: You will hear an organiser welcoming visitors to a winter festival held on a frozen canal in Ottawa.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to Canal Frost Weekend. My name's Nadia, and I'm one of the organisers. We're delighted that so many of you have braved the cold, and I'd like to take a few minutes to tell you what's on, and to give you some practical information, so you can make the most of the next two days.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: The festival is spread along about two kilometres of the canal, and it's divided into five areas. Let me start at the western end, where you'll find the skating loop. The ice is smooth and well maintained, and every hour, on the hour, our instructors run a lesson for beginners. It's free, and you don't need to book. If you've never been on skates before, this is the place to start, and you'll be amazed how quickly you pick it up. Skates can be hired from the hut by the entrance, although I should say that the queue is usually long on Saturday afternoons.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Next to the skating loop is the market tent. Here you can buy food from local producers, such as maple syrup, smoked fish and pastries, as well as crafts made by artists from the region. Many of the stalls accept cards, but a few only take cash, so it's worth carrying some.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Moving east, we come to the sculpture park, which is for many people the highlight of the festival. Teams of carvers from across Canada have spent the past week turning huge blocks of ice into sculptures, and over the weekend you can watch some of them finishing their work. They'll be giving carving demonstrations every afternoon, and you can ask them questions. Please don't touch the sculptures, though. Fingers and gloves damage the surface.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: At the centre of the festival is the main stage, where there's live music from local bands all weekend. The line-up on the printed programme has changed slightly, so do check the screen beside the stage, because a couple of the Sunday acts have swapped times.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: And finally, along the eastern bank you'll find the warming huts. These are small wooden shelters, each designed by a different architecture student, and inside you can warm up beside a heater and have a free hot drink, thanks to our sponsors. They're very popular with families, so be prepared to wait a few minutes at busy times.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Now, some practical points. How do you get here? I'd strongly advise leaving your car at home. The streets beside the canal are closed to traffic for the whole weekend, and the nearest car parks fill up by ten o'clock. The best way to arrive is on one of our free shuttle buses, which leave from the central station every fifteen minutes. Some people prefer to walk from the city centre, but it's about forty minutes, and it can be very cold, so most visitors choose the bus.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: As for tickets, I'm happy to say that entry to the festival is completely free. However, some of the activities have a small charge, such as skate hire and the guided night tour, and the food and drink in the market tent are of course not free either.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Next, what should you wear? Everyone knows that you need warm clothes, and I hope you're all wearing several layers. But my most important advice is about footwear. The paths between the areas are covered in packed snow and ice, and they get very slippery by the end of the day. Please wear proper boots with a good grip, rather than trainers or smart shoes. We've seen a few sprained ankles in previous years, and we'd like to avoid that this time.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Tomorrow evening, there's the fireworks display, which has always been the most popular event of the weekend. It was originally planned for eight o'clock, but we've moved it to nine o'clock, so that it doesn't clash with the children's lantern parade, which will finish at about half past eight. The best place to watch is on the bridge, but it gets crowded, so the banks on either side are also excellent.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: Finally, something new this year. We've developed a festival app, which you can download for free before you arrive. It has a map of the site, but the main feature is that it shows the waiting times for the most popular activities, so you can see at a glance whether it's worth joining the queue for the skating lessons or whether you'd be better off visiting the market first. If you have any trouble with it, there's a help desk next to the main stage.

transcript.speaker: Nadia
transcript.text: That's all from me. If you have any questions, ask any of our volunteers in the orange jackets. Please enjoy the festival, stay warm, and thank you for coming.

sections.title: A history project on the Victorian goldfields
sections.context: You will hear two history students, Leila and Ravi, discussing their project with their tutor, Professor Wallace.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: Hello, Leila, hello, Ravi. Come in and sit down. I've read your outline for the history project, so let's talk through it. You're focusing on Chinese miners on the Victorian goldfields, is that right?

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: That's right. We wanted to look at their daily lives in the eighteen fifties and sixties, rather than just the big events.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: It's a good topic. What made you choose it?

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: Well, honestly, we first thought about the Eureka uprising, because it's the famous one. But Leila found that the local museum has a collection of objects from the Chinese camps, and almost nobody has written about it.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: Yes, I went to look at it last month. The curator told me that hardly any students ever ask about it. So we thought we could actually add something new.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: That's the best reason to choose a topic. Now, what about your sources? Where will the information come from?

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: Mostly from the state archive, which holds the court records and the newspapers. The problem is that the archive has quite limited opening hours, and it's an hour's drive from here.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: And the other difficulty is that a lot of the documents are in Chinese. We can't read them, and we don't have a translator.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: You're right to worry about that. I'd suggest you contact the Asian languages department. Some of their postgraduates are looking for projects like this one, and they might be happy to help with a few key documents. As for the opening hours, I wouldn't worry, because you can book a reading room and the staff will bring the files to you.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: Oh, that's useful. I thought we had to turn up and wait.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: Not at all. Now, for the section on daily life, which sources will you use?

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: We were planning to use the newspaper advertisements, because they show what miners were buying and selling. And possibly letters, because some of the families kept them.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: But the letters are in private collections, aren't they? We'd have to contact the families, and that could take months.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: Exactly. I'd skip the letters. The court records are a much better source, because they list the names, the jobs and the addresses of the people involved. And the photographs held at the museum are excellent, so I'd definitely include those. The newspaper advertisements are interesting, but you'll find they mostly describe the European customers, so they won't help much with the Chinese miners.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: All right. Court records and photographs, then.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: One more worry. Some of the court records mention people only by English nicknames, and the spelling changes from one document to the next.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: That's a classic problem. Keep a spreadsheet with every spelling you find, and note the date and the page. Over time patterns emerge, and you can often match one person across several documents.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: We could divide the work. I'll take the court records from the eighteen fifties, and Leila can take the following decade.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: A sensible plan, although I'd suggest you both read a few records from each decade first, so that your methods are consistent. Otherwise, your two halves may read like two different essays.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: Good point. We'll meet every Thursday to compare notes.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: Excellent. That kind of routine saves a lot of trouble near the deadline.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: Good. Now, how are you going to present the work in class?

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: I'd like to do a short film, with photographs and a voiceover. It would look much more interesting than slides.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: I'm not so sure. A film takes ages to make, and we have to submit the essay as well. I'd prefer a poster, and then we could each talk for five minutes.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: I think the poster is the more realistic choice, but Ravi, you can still use a few of your best images on it. Make sure it isn't crowded with text.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: Fair enough. A poster it is.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: One more thing, about the essay itself. The limit is three thousand words, and students nearly always try to cover too much. Choose three or four strong examples and treat them in depth, rather than trying to mention everything.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: That makes sense. Could you suggest some books to start with? We found a lot, but we aren't sure which are reliable.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: Certainly. Let's go through your list. The first one, the general history of the goldfields, is well written, but it's very broad, and it only has a few pages about the Chinese miners. It's fine for background, but you won't find much detail.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: And the second one, the book by the local historian?

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: That one is the opposite. It's rather old, from the nineteen sixties, and some of its conclusions have been challenged, so I'd use it carefully. But the third one is very good, because it includes tables of statistics from the census, showing how many miners came from each region. You'll definitely want that.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: Great, we'll start with the third one, then.

transcript.speaker: Professor Wallace
transcript.text: Excellent. Send me a draft of the first section in two weeks, and I'll give you feedback. And please let me know if the archive staff cause you any trouble.

transcript.speaker: Ravi
transcript.text: Thank you, Professor Wallace.

sections.title: Urban heat islands
sections.context: You will hear a lecturer in environmental planning talking about urban heat islands.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is about urban heat islands, a phenomenon that affects almost every large city, and which will matter more and more as the climate warms. A heat island is simply an urban area that is noticeably warmer than the rural land around it. The difference is largest at night. On a calm, clear night, the centre of a big city can be up to 7 degrees Celsius warmer than the countryside nearby. During the day the gap is smaller, usually two or three degrees, but it still has a real effect on how people feel and how much energy they use.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: So why does this happen? There are several causes, and it's important to understand each of them, because the solutions depend on them. The first is the materials we build with. Roads, car parks and roofs are mostly made of dark materials such as asphalt and concrete. These absorb a lot of the sun's energy during the day, and then release it slowly after sunset, which is why the nights stay warm. A grass field, by contrast, reflects more light and stores much less heat.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: The second cause is the loss of vegetation. Plants cool the air in two ways. They provide shade, and they release water vapour through their leaves, which is rather like sweating. When a city replaces a park with a paved car park, it loses both. Studies in Sydney and Vancouver have found that suburbs with plenty of trees can be several degrees cooler than similar suburbs without them.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: The third cause is waste heat. Every air conditioner moves heat from inside a building to the outside, and the engines of vehicles produce a lot of heat as well. In a busy city centre in summer, this adds up to a significant amount, and it creates a vicious circle: the hotter it gets, the more people use air conditioning, which makes the streets hotter still.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: The fourth cause is the shape of the city itself. Tall buildings built close together form what we call street canyons. In a canyon, heat that is released from the walls and the road gets trapped between the buildings, and there's very little wind to carry it away. At night, the buildings also block the view of the sky, so the heat can't radiate away into space as easily.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: Now, why does it matter? It isn't only about comfort. Heat waves are one of the leading causes of weather-related deaths in Australia, and elderly people and young children are most at risk. Hot nights are especially dangerous, because the body doesn't get a chance to recover. There are also economic effects, because electricity demand rises sharply in hot weather, and power networks can fail.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: Let's turn to solutions. The simplest is to change the colour of surfaces. A cool roof is one that reflects most of the sunlight instead of absorbing it, and the cheapest way to make one is to paint a normal roof white. In trials, white roofs have lowered indoor temperatures by several degrees, and the cost is very small compared with air conditioning.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: A second solution is the green roof, which is a roof covered with soil and plants. On a hot day, the surface of a green roof can be up to 30 degrees cooler than a conventional dark roof. Green roofs also absorb rainwater, which reduces flooding, and they provide a habitat for insects and birds. They're heavier and more expensive to build, however, so many cities use rules and incentives to encourage them. In Toronto, for example, a by-law requires a green roof on every new building with a floor area of more than 2000 square metres. It was the first rule of its kind in North America.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: A third solution is simply to plant more trees. Melbourne has an urban forest strategy, which aims to increase the tree canopy to 40 percent of the city by 2040. That's an ambitious target, because many of the city's older trees are dying in the drought, and planting trees in the middle of a busy street is surprisingly difficult. The roots need space, water and protection from traffic.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: Finally, a word about how researchers measure all this. In the past, scientists relied on thermometers at a small number of weather stations, which gave a very limited picture. Today, they use thermal images taken by satellites and aircraft, which show the temperature of every street and every roof. Planners can use these maps to identify the hottest neighbourhoods, which are very often the poorest, and to decide where new trees and cool roofs will have the greatest effect.

transcript.speaker: Doctor Tran
transcript.text: For next week, please read the two case studies on the course page, and consider this question. If a city has a limited budget, should it invest in trees, in cool roofs, or in helping people buy air conditioners? There's no single right answer, and I'd like you to be ready to defend your choice.
